  trusted server environment (`ENTIRE_BRAIN_GRAPH_BINARY`, default `entire`), never
  from a client argument, and constrains the index path to the bound repo root
  unless `ENTIRE_BRAIN_MCP_ALLOW_ANY_PATH` is set.

  checkout and execute the same manifest snapshot they validated. This closes the confused-deputy path where

  every other project on the machine. The plain `entire brain ...` CLI keeps its
  cross-repo verbs: a human at a terminal is not the confused deputy.

`fuzz_test.go` provides panic-invariant fuzz harnesses for the untrusted parsers:
MCP framing, the entire-graph NDJSON stream, the `embed_store` binary loader, the
distilled fact-line parser, and the document-conversation parser. Run e.g.:

```sh
go test ./internal/cli -run '^$' -fuzz FuzzScanSemanticStream -fuzztime 30s
```

81				out = append(out, string(runes[i:j]))
82			}
83			for k := i; k+1 < j; k++ {
84				out = append(out, string(runes[k:k+2]))
85			}
86			i = j
87		}
88		flushPlain()
89		return out
90	}
91	
92	func isCJKRune(r rune) bool {
93		return unicode.In(r, unicode.Han, unicode.Hiragana, unicode.Katakana, unicode.Hangul)
94	}
95	
96	// factPlainTokens lowercases and splits on non-alphanumerics (underscore
97	// kept), the tokenization the retrieval eval measured.
98	func factPlainTokens(text string) []string {
99		lower := strings.ToLower(text)
100		return strings.FieldsFunc(lower, func(r rune) bool {
101			return !(r >= 'a' && r <= 'z' || r >= '0' && r <= '9' || r == '_')
102		})
103	}
104	
105	// factQueryTerms are the deduplicated query tokens, with the history stopword
106	// list applied so "how does the" carries no weight. Like factSearchTokens on
107	// the document side, the query unions the ASCII plain tokens with the
108	// Unicode-aware normalizer's tokens: the plain tokenizer alone yields nothing
109	// for CJK/Cyrillic queries and truncates accented words at the accent.
110	func factQueryTerms(query string) []string {
111		seen := map[string]struct{}{}
112		var terms []string
113		add := func(t string) {
114			if len(t) < 2 || historyQueryStopword(t) {
115				return
116			}
117			if _, ok := seen[t]; ok {
118				return
119			}
120			seen[t] = struct{}{}
121			terms = append(terms, t)
122		}
123		for _, t := range factPlainTokens(query) {
124			add(t)
125		}
126		for _, t := range strings.Fields(normalizeHistorySearchText(query)) {
127			for _, piece := range expandCJKBigrams(t) {
128				add(piece)
129			}
130		}
131		return terms
132	}
133	
134	// bm25Corpus holds the per-call corpus statistics BM25 needs. Recomputed per
135	// query over the candidate set — ponytail: O(corpus) per query, measured at
136	// well under a millisecond for 1,209 facts; an inverted index is the upgrade
137	// path if fact counts grow by orders of magnitude.
138	type bm25Corpus struct {
139		docTokens [][]string
140		df        map[string]int
141		avgLen    float64
142	}
143	
144	func newBM25Corpus(facts []factRecord) bm25Corpus {
145		c := bm25Corpus{
146			docTokens: make([][]string, len(facts)),
147			df:        make(map[string]int, len(facts)*8),
148		}
149		total := 0
150		for i, f := range facts {
151			tokens := factSearchTokens(f)
152			c.docTokens[i] = tokens
153			total += len(tokens)
154			seen := make(map[string]struct{}, len(tokens))
155			for _, t := range tokens {
156				if _, ok := seen[t]; ok {
157					continue
158				}
159				seen[t] = struct{}{}
160				c.df[t]++
161			}
162		}
163		if len(facts) > 0 {
164			c.avgLen = float64(total) / float64(len(facts))
165		}
166		return c
167	}
168	
169	// bm25Score is the Okapi BM25 text relevance of candidate i for the query
170	// terms, over this corpus.
171	func (c bm25Corpus) bm25Score(i int, terms []string) float64 {
172		tokens := c.docTokens[i]
173		if len(tokens) == 0 || len(terms) == 0 {
174			return 0
175		}
176		tf := make(map[string]int, len(tokens))
177		for _, t := range tokens {
178			tf[t]++
179		}
180		n := float64(len(c.docTokens))
181		score := 0.0
182		for _, term := range terms {
183			f := float64(tf[term])
184			if f == 0 {
185				continue
186			}
187			idf := math.Log((n-float64(c.df[term])+0.5)/(float64(c.df[term])+0.5) + 1)
188			norm := 1 - bm25B + bm25B*float64(len(tokens))/c.avgLen
189			score += idf * f * (bm25K1 + 1) / (f + bm25K1*norm)
190		}
191		return score
192	}
193	
194	// factBM25Score is the full facts ranking score: BM25 text relevance plus the
195	// two previously measured boosts (shared code locus, closed-negative kind).
196	// Boosts apply only to facts that already match, so neither creates a match on
197	// its own — same contract as the scorer this replaces.
198	func factBM25Score(f factRecord, c bm25Corpus, i int, terms []string, queryLocus []string) float64 {
199		score := c.bm25Score(i, terms)
200		if score <= 0 {
201			return 0
202		}
203		if overlap := locusOverlapTokens(queryLocus, factLocusOf(f)); overlap > 0 {
204			score += float64(overlap) * bm25LocusBoost
205		}
206		if factKindOrInferred(f) == factKindClosedNegative {
207			score += bm25ClosedNegativeBoost
208		}
209		return score
210	}
211	
212	// filterFacts narrows candidates by taxonomy path prefix, fact kind, and
213	// minimum update time. Zero values skip that filter. A path prefix matches a
214	// whole segment boundary: "architecture.sync" matches "architecture.sync" and
215	// "architecture.sync.auth", not "architecture.syncextra".
216	func filterFacts(facts []factRecord, pathPrefix, kind string, since time.Time) []factRecord {
217		if pathPrefix == "" && kind == "" && since.IsZero() {
218			return facts
219		}
220		out := make([]factRecord, 0, len(facts))
221		for _, f := range facts {
222			if kind != "" && f.Kind != kind {
223				continue
224			}
225			if !since.IsZero() && f.UpdatedAt.Before(since) {
226				continue
227			}
228			if pathPrefix != "" && !factMatchesPathPrefix(f, pathPrefix) {
229				continue
230			}
231			out = append(out, f)
232		}
233		return out
234	}
235	
236	func factMatchesPathPrefix(f factRecord, prefix string) bool {
237		for _, p := range f.Paths {
238			if p == prefix || strings.HasPrefix(p, prefix+".") {
239				return true
240			}
241		}
242		return false
243	}

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ MCP write tools are omitted because your organization has MCP Write Access disabled. An organization administrator can enable MCP Write Access in Organization Settings. Reconnect afterward so your client refreshes its tools. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your one lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

entries.name: mcp__linear__create_attachment_from_upload
entries.description:
Link an already-uploaded Linear assetUrl to an existing issue as an attachment.
Uploaded files appear in the issue's Resources; they are not native Linear Documents. For written findings or proposals, prefer updating the issue description or using save_document with issue to create an editable Linear Document, unless the user requests a file. The upload workflow creates the Resources link; do not also add the upload URL to save_issue's links field. To revise a file, upload a replacement. To remove its Resources link, use delete_attachment with the attachment ID returned by get_issue. These tools do not edit uploaded file contents, permanently delete stored files, or inspect or change per-file permissions. Explain these limits when relevant.

Use this only after:
1. prepare_attachment_upload returned an assetUrl and uploadRequest.
2. The client successfully PUT raw file bytes to uploadRequest.url.

This tool does not upload file content. It only creates the Linear attachment row.
If the direct upload failed or the signed URL expired, rerun prepare_attachment_upload and upload again.

issue.description: Issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). P-prefixed identifiers (e.g., P-ENG-123) are projects, not issues

assetUrl.description: Linear upload assetUrl returned by prepare_attachment_upload

title.description: Attachment title. Defaults to filename or asset URL

entries.name: mcp__linear__prepare_attachment_upload
entries.description:
Prepare a direct Linear file upload for an existing issue.
Uploaded files appear in the issue's Resources; they are not native Linear Documents. For written findings or proposals, prefer updating the issue description or using save_document with issue to create an editable Linear Document, unless the user requests a file. The upload workflow creates the Resources link; do not also add the upload URL to save_issue's links field. To revise a file, upload a replacement. To remove its Resources link, use delete_attachment with the attachment ID returned by get_issue. These tools do not edit uploaded file contents, permanently delete stored files, or inspect or change per-file permissions. Explain these limits when relevant.

Workflow:
1. Call this tool with issue, filename, contentType, and size.
2. Upload raw bytes with PUT to uploadRequest.url outside MCP.
3. All headers in uploadRequest.headers are part of the signed request, so send them verbatim.
4. After PUT succeeds, call create_attachment_from_upload with assetUrl to link it to the issue.

Do not base64-encode or transform the file. Use curl --data-binary @path or fetch(url, { method: 'PUT', body: blob }).
Omitting or modifying any signed header, including casing, will return HTTP 403.
The signed URL must be used within 60 seconds or it will expire.

Upload sequencing:
Prepare, PUT, and finalize one file before calling this tool for another file.
Do not batch multiple prepare_attachment_upload calls before starting the PUTs because earlier signed URLs can expire while later files are prepared.

Example:
curl -X PUT --data-binary @file.png \
  -H "content-type: image/png" \
  -H "x-goog-content-length-range: N,N" \
  -H "cache-control: public, max-age=31536000" \
  -H 'Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="file.png"' \
  "<uploadRequest.url>"

issue.description: Issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). P-prefixed identifiers (e.g., P-ENG-123) are projects, not issues

filename.description: Filename for the upload, e.g. screenshot.png

contentType.description: MIME type, e.g. image/png or application/pdf

size.description: Exact file size in bytes. Must be smaller than 2 GB.

title.description: Suggested attachment title for the finalize step

subtitle.description: Suggested attachment subtitle for the finalize step

content.text:
Store fixed, and the re-profile rewrites the optimization story. Brief went **13.2s → 4.0s warm** — most of what I called "optimization targets" was store damage.

**What was broken, and what I did:**
- **Facts: unbounded duplication bug (real product bug, still in main).** `loadAllFactBranches` (`internal/cli/facts_manifest.go:14`) groups records by the `branch` field *on each record*, not the directory. A stray dir — `facts/evis-cor-2126-per-fact-sync-782a0c9e`, 958 records all stamped `branch: main`, leftover from the per-fact-sync work — got merged into main on **every refresh**, and reclassify rewrote main's file with +958 duplicate ids each time (I reproduced it: dedupe → refresh → 964 → 1,922). `facts gc` can't repair it and doctor's suggested remedy (refresh + re-distill) makes it worse. I quarantined the stray dir beside the brain root, deduped main 3,838 → 964 records (backup kept), and verified a refresh now stays clean. Code fix needed: key by directory or dedupe in `writeFacts`.
- **Semantic index stale** → rebuilt via refresh (the provider parse took ~5 min — that's the "why a cache must exist" number, live).
- **Entity index "failed"** → frozen state from the watch daemon's last tick 98h ago, *before* the graph plugin was installed Oct 16. Backfill succeeded immediately.
- **History FTS stale** → rewarmed; doctor now reports facts ok, semantic ok, history ok.

**Re-profiled brief (same task, warm):**

| Stage | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| total | 13,174 ms | **4,021 ms** |
| history.indexed_rank | 7,923 ms | **148 ms** |
| status_build_state | 3,068 ms | 2,317 ms |
| semantic.context + tests | 1,351 ms | 1,423 ms |

So the honest correction: the 7.9s history ranking was the degraded raw-scan path behind a stale FTS cache — healthy path is 45× faster, not a target. On a healthy store brief is **58% status embedding** (2.3s + 41KB of the 50KB packet) and **35% semantic read** — and the semantic read scans all 230k index rows *twice* (context and tests each take in=230,732) to emit 24 items. Those two are the real optimization list, in that order. The semantic-pipeline necessity question is unchanged — still unmeasured value — but its read cost is now the #2 line, which strengthens the case for running the cheap brief-with/without eval.

**Left for you:** `entire-brain setup` — the watch daemon unit is stale (that dead daemon is *why* the store rotted unnoticed), and the recorded `setup semantic/entity index` errors only clear when setup re-runs. Both facts recorded in Brain; the duplication bug probably deserves its own trail — say the word.

input.title: Brain: every refresh duplicates facts when a stray branch dir holds records stamped for another branch
input.description:
## Problem

`loadAllFactBranches` (`internal/cli/facts_manifest.go`) groups fact records by the `branch` field **on each record**, not by the on-disk branch directory. If any branch directory contains records stamped with another branch's name, every `refresh` merges them into that branch's slice, and `reclassifyAllFactBranches` rewrites the target branch's `facts.ndjson` with the merged set. Nothing dedupes by id, so the file grows by the stray record count on **every refresh**, without bound.

Observed on the entire-brain dogfood store (2026-10-19): `facts/evis-cor-2126-per-fact-sync-782a0c9e/` held 958 records all stamped `branch: main` (leftover from per-fact hosted sync development). Main's `facts.ndjson` had grown to 3,838 lines for 964 unique ids (~4 copies each). Each additional refresh appended exactly 958 more records. Reproduced deterministically: dedupe to 964 → one refresh → 1,922.

## Impact

- `recall`/`query` candidates contain repeated facts and BM25 document frequencies are inflated (`loadFacts` returns all lines; no dedupe anywhere downstream).
- `doctor` flags it ("fact ids are not unique") but its remedy — "run `entire brain refresh` and re-distill" — makes it worse.
- `facts gc` cannot repair it (only prunes retracted/superseded).
- Store and hosted-sync payloads grow without bound.

## Fix options

1. Key `loadAllFactBranches` by directory (the slug is lossy, but grouping by record field is what makes a stray record contagious), or
2. Dedupe by id in `writeFacts` (last record wins), or both.
3. Also fix the `doctor` remedy text, and consider a `facts gc` mode that repairs duplicate ids.

A regression test should cover: branch dir A containing records stamped branch B, then refresh twice → branch B's file must not grow.

## Manual repair applied to the dogfood store (for reference)

Quarantined the stray dir to `quarantine-stray-facts-evis-cor-2126-782a0c9e` beside the brain root and rewrote main's `facts.ndjson` keeping the last record per id (backup: `facts.ndjson.bak-dedupe-20261019`). Verified a subsequent refresh no longer grows the file and `doctor` reports facts ok.

{"id":"COR-2192","uuid":"08522d4c-c947-4313-a149-7988bc3a7767","title":"Brain: every refresh duplicates facts when a stray branch dir holds records stamped for another branch","description":"## Problem

`loadAllFactBranches` (`internal/cli/facts_manifest.go`) groups fact records by the `branch` field **on each record**, not by the on-disk branch directory. If any branch directory contains records stamped with another branch's name, every `refresh` merges them into that branch's slice, and `reclassifyAllFactBranches` rewrites the target branch's `facts.ndjson` with the merged set. Nothing dedupes by id, so the file grows by the stray record count on **every refresh**, without bound.

Observed on the entire-brain dogfood store (2026-10-19): `facts/evis-cor-2126-per-fact-sync-782a0c9e/` held 958 records all stamped `branch: main` (leftover from per-fact hosted sync development). Main's `facts.ndjson` had grown to 3,838 lines for 964 unique ids (\~4 copies each). Each additional refresh appended exactly 958 more records. Reproduced deterministically: dedupe to 964 → one refresh → 1,922.

## Impact

* `recall`/`query` candidates contain repeated facts and BM25 document frequencies are inflated (`loadFacts` returns all lines; no dedupe anywhere downstream).
* `doctor` flags it ("fact ids are not unique") but its remedy — "run `entire brain refresh` and re-distill" — makes it worse.
* `facts gc` cannot repair it (only prunes retracted/superseded).
* Store and hosted-sync payloads grow without bound.

## Fix options

1. Key `loadAllFactBranches` by directory (the slug is lossy, but grouping by record field is what makes a stray record contagious), or
2. Dedupe by id in `writeFacts` (last record wins), or both.
3. Also fix the `doctor` remedy text, and consider a `facts gc` mode that repairs duplicate ids.

A regression test should cover: branch dir A containing records stamped branch B, then refresh twice → branch B's file must not grow.

content.text:
Ticket filed: [COR-2192](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2192/brain-every-refresh-duplicates-facts-when-a-stray-branch-dir-holds) (Core backlog), with the root cause, repro, impact, fix options, and the manual repair record.

**What `status_build_state` is:** the first stage of every brief — `buildBrainStatusReport` (`internal/cli/agent_surface.go:4438`), the same machinery behind `entire brain status`. Its output becomes the packet's status section (the 41KB one).

**Why 2.3s:** `status` runs it in lightweight mode; brief runs it strict ("other read surfaces retain strict artifact validation"). I measured the lightweight path at 0.53s, so ~1.8s is strict-only auditing, and the bulk of that is one call: strict freshness runs `verifiedSnapshotSummary`, which **scans the entire 158MB `snapshot.ndjson`** to re-verify its header and record counts — on every brief. The irony is that this verification *is* memoized (`semanticIntegrityMemo`, keyed on path + size/mtime), but the memo is in-process and every brief is a fresh CLI process, so it never hits. The remaining strict extras are smaller: SQLite store count validation, a full integrity read of all 49 branch fact files, and the conversation-projection audit. The shared ~0.5s base is git live-state (status + changed-symbol hints), manifest load, hosted status, and daemon inspection.

So the 2.3s buys a guarantee — "never serve a brief from a corrupt store" — paid in full on every invocation because the cache that should amortize it dies with the process. Three fix shapes, cheapest first:

1. **Persist the integrity memo to disk** keyed on (path, size, mtime, repo key) — keeps the guarantee, drops the rescan to ~0 after the first brief per snapshot. Smallest change.
2. Have brief use the lightweight report (presence checks only) — fastest, but weakens the guarantee brief deliberately opted into.
3. Verify in the background and stamp the packet with "verified as of X".

Given yesterday's finding that the store rotted for days with nobody noticing, I'd keep the strict check and do option 1. Want me to take that on?

content.text:
**Issue.** Before serving a brief, Brain proves the semantic snapshot isn't corrupt by reading all 158MB of it and checking the record counts against the manifest. That proof takes ~1.8s. There's already a cache for it (`semanticIntegrityMemo`), but it lives in process memory — and every `brief` is a new process, so the cache is always empty and the 158MB rescan happens every time.

**Why caching is sound.** The file can't change without its size or mtime changing (every writer replaces it atomically). So "I verified *this exact file identity* once" is as good as verifying it again.

**Solution.** Write the verdict to a small file next to the snapshot after the first successful verification: `(snapshot path, size, mtime, repo key) → verified`. On the next brief, if the identity matches, skip the scan; if anything differs, re-verify and rewrite.

**Why it fixes it.** First brief after a refresh pays the 1.8s once; every later brief does one stat call instead of a 158MB read. Same guarantee, ~2.3s → ~0.5s per brief.

The one honest caveat: mtime+size is a heuristic, not a hash — a byte-flip from disk corruption that changes neither would go unnoticed. That's exactly the trust the in-process memo already accepts; the disk cache just extends it across processes.

content.text:
Yes, that's the flow — one correction on who owns what:

```
setup / refresh
  1. Brain invokes entire-graph, which parses the repo (~5 min on this repo)
  2. graph streams NDJSON records to Brain; Brain saves that stream
     as its own snapshot.ndjson (158MB)          ← Brain's copy, not graph's
  3. Brain ingests the snapshot into semantic.sqlite (~200MB)

brief
  4. Brain queries semantic.sqlite (the 0.7s context + 0.7s tests scans)
  5. Brain re-verifies snapshot.ndjson first (the 1.8s we just discussed)
```

So Brain stores **two** derived artifacts from one parse: the raw stream it kept (snapshot) and the sqlite store it built from it. And separately, entire-graph maintains its *own* committed-tree cache for `entire graph query` — that's the duplication we talked about earlier: the same parse materialized twice, once in each plugin, because Brain's store predates graph being split out as its own surface.

Which also sharpens your "why do we need this" question: the honest framing is not "does Brain need a semantic index" but "does Brain need *its own copy* when graph already keeps one it could query."

But some things wouldn't disappear — the history/entities index still needs a graph diff per commit, and incremental parsing (not just raw full-parse speed) is what actually matters for keeping things fresh during editing versus initial repo setup. Making parsing genuinely fast seems very plausible, since tree-sitter itself runs at MB/s and the real bottleneck is likely relation resolution and lack of parallelism rather than parsing itself.

Then I notice a separate cheap win: over half the indexed symbols — 29,940 of 51,929 — are actually JSON, with another 1,914 being markdown sections, meaning most of the symbol index is non-code and probably low-value to extract in the first place.

For the answer, I want to be concise: confirm that fast parsing does unlock deleting Brain's redundant cache, note that duplication itself is a design choice fixable independent of parse speed, and flag that so much of the index being JSON/markdown suggests the parser is doing a lot of low-value work — without actually starting any of that work now.

content.text:
Yes — that's the right read of the causal chain, with one refinement: parse latency justifies *a* cache, but the *duplication* (Brain's second copy) is a separate design choice you can fix today without touching parse speed. Fast parse mostly removes the fear that makes every consumer cache defensively.

What a fast parse (seconds, not minutes) would let you delete or shrink:

- Brain's snapshot retention + the 158MB re-verification (reparse is cheaper than proving a cache honest)
- Most of the freshness/staleness machinery — "stale" stops being a dangerous state when recovery is seconds
- The 900s-timeout class of failures and the setup-ordering fragility (the daemon-died-before-plugin-installed rot we just repaired)
- Entities backfill pain (it's parse-per-commit underneath)

What it wouldn't fix by itself: Brain querying its own sqlite copy instead of graph's surface — that's delegation (option B), doable regardless.

And there's a concrete lead on *why* it's slow: look at the coverage numbers from doctor — **29,940 of 51,929 symbols are JSON records and 1,914 are markdown sections**. More than half the index is non-code, and the 30k CONFIGURES relations come from that. The parser is spending its time extracting structure from benchmark JSON fixtures and doc files. Likely wins, in order: stop deep-parsing non-code file types (or make it opt-in), parallelize across files (it ran at ~74% of one core), and do incremental re-parse of changed files only. None of those are exotic.

Sequencing I'd suggest: profile entire-graph's parse on this repo first — if it confirms the non-code/single-thread story, that's a cheap fix with a huge lever, and the simplification of Brain's machinery becomes a follow-on rather than a bet. That work lives in the entire-graph repo, though — want me to set up that profiling as the next task there?

Stream the whole graph: files, symbols, and relations (bulk NDJSON)

Usage:
  entire graph snapshot --repo . --format ndjson|compact-ndjson [--worktree]

One header record, then file, external-endpoint, symbol, and relation records, streamed so memory stays bounded. Superset of symbols + edges + files — use it to ingest the full graph into an agent memory or a store such as Entire Brain. compact-ndjson is a complete-snapshot-only local artifact that can be read by snapshot-query.

Flags:
  --repo <path>           Repository (default: current repo)
  --format ndjson|compact-ndjson
                          Output format; compact requires a complete snapshot (default: ndjson)
  --worktree              Stream the working tree instead of HEAD (never cached)
  --progress              Emit progress events to stderr
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                          Parsing depth (default: full)
  --ignore-file <path>    Extra gitignore-style exclude rules (repeatable)
  --include-file <path>   Re-include ignored paths (gitignore-style; not an allowlist)

Examples:
  entire graph snapshot --repo . --format ndjson
  entire graph snapshot --repo . --format compact-ndjson > graph.compact.ndjson

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Aggregate macOS `sample` output: top-of-stack leaves and heaviest call-tree paths."""
import re, sys, collections

path = sys.argv[1]
text = open(path).read()

idx = text.find("Sort by top of stack")
if idx >= 0:
    leaves = []
    for line in text[idx:].splitlines()[1:]:
        m = re.match(r"\s+(\S.*?)\s+\(in ([^)]+)\)\s.*?(\d+)\s*$", line)
        if not m:
            m2 = re.match(r"\s+(\S.*?)\s+\(in ([^)]+)\)\s+(\d+)$", line)
            if not m2:
                continue
            m = m2
        leaves.append((int(m.group(3)), m.group(1), m.group(2)))
    leaves.sort(reverse=True)
    print("== top of stack (self samples)")
    for n, fn, lib in leaves[:18]:
        print(f"  {n:>7}  {fn}  ({lib})")

# Heaviest root-to-leaf path: follow max-weight child in the call tree section.
print("\n== heaviest call paths (indented tree, weight-sorted lines)")
tree = []
for line in text.splitlines():
    m = re.match(r"^(\s+)(\d+)\s+(.*?)\s+\(in ([^)]+)\)", line)
    if m:
        depth = len(m.group(1))
        tree.append((depth, int(m.group(2)), m.group(3), m.group(4)))
# print entries above a weight threshold, preserving order (shows structure)
if tree:
    maxw = max(w for _, w, _, _ in tree)
    thr = maxw * 0.15
    shown = 0
    for depth, w, fn, lib in tree:
        if w >= thr and shown < 60:
            print(f"{' ' * (depth // 2)}{w:>7} {fn} ({lib})")
            shown += 1

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Aggregate macOS `sample` output: top-of-stack leaves and heaviest call-tree paths."""
import re, sys, collections

path = sys.argv[1]
text = open(path).read()

idx = text.find("Sort by top of stack")
if idx >= 0:
    leaves = []
    for line in text[idx:].splitlines()[1:]:
        m = re.match(r"\s+(\S.*?)\s+\(in ([^)]+)\)\s.*?(\d+)\s*$", line)
        if not m:
            m2 = re.match(r"\s+(\S.*?)\s+\(in ([^)]+)\)\s+(\d+)$", line)
            if not m2:
                continue
            m = m2
        leaves.append((int(m.group(3)), m.group(1), m.group(2)))
    leaves.sort(reverse=True)
    print("== top of stack (self samples)")
    for n, fn, lib in leaves[:18]:
        print(f"  {n:>7}  {fn}  ({lib})")

# Heaviest root-to-leaf path: follow max-weight child in the call tree section.
print("\n== heaviest call paths (indented tree, weight-sorted lines)")
tree = []
for line in text.splitlines():
    m = re.match(r"^(\s+)(\d+)\s+(.*?)\s+\(in ([^)]+)\)", line)
    if m:
        depth = len(m.group(1))
        tree.append((depth, int(m.group(2)), m.group(3), m.group(4)))
# print entries above a weight threshold, preserving order (shows structure)
if tree:
    maxw = max(w for _, w, _, _ in tree)
    thr = maxw * 0.15
    shown = 0
    for depth, w, fn, lib in tree:
        if w >= thr and shown < 60:
            print(f"{' ' * (depth // 2)}{w:>7} {fn} ({lib})")
            shown += 1

# For each sample stack line in the call tree, attribute regexp leaf weight to the

total_regexp = 0
for line in open("/tmp/dev-sample-early.txt"):
    m = re.match(r"^(\s+)(\d+)\s+(.*?)\s+\(in ([^)]+)\)", line)

        stack.pop()

        # attribute to nearest sem.* ancestor, count once at the regexp subtree root
        if not any(name.startswith("regexp") for d, name in stack[:-1]):

content.text:
Baseline and profiling complete. Here's the full picture.

## End-to-end baseline (this repo: 1,817 files, 52k symbols)

| Step | Time | Peak RSS | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| graph parse, **installed v0.4.0**, full, cold | 70.7s | 1.53GB | 125MB NDJSON |
| graph parse, **main (dev build)**, full, cold | **34.3s** | 0.58GB | 130MB |
| graph parse, main, `--profile fast`, cold | 10.3s | — | 83MB |
| graph parse, main, `--profile syntax-only`, cold | 2.8s | — | 55MB |
| graph, any profile, **warm commit-keyed cache** | **1.0s** | 0.46GB | byte-identical |
| Brain ingest (filter + write 158MB snapshot + build sqlite), graph warm | 35.7s | 0.46GB | ~360MB on disk |
| Brain strict verify (every brief) | 1.8s | — | — |
| Brief semantic read | 1.4s | — | — |

So cold setup today is ~71s graph + ~36s Brain ≈ **107s**, not 5 minutes — the 5-minute impression was the full refresh doing everything (history, facts, patterns, docs) on a damaged store.

## Where the parse time actually goes (pprof, dev build)

- **42% of CPU: regex-based relation extraction** (`forEachRelation`) — not parsing. The top consumers are DATA_FLOWS analysis (`returnFlowCalls` 17%, `expressionAssignedReturnFlows` 5%), deep call resolution (`receiverCallRelations` 10%), and `staticStringConstants` 5%. The sem package has 614 regex compile sites; Phase 2 re-reads every function body and runs regex families over it.
- **Tree-sitter parsing is only 5.6%.** The "parser" is fast; the semantic enrichment is slow.
- **28% is scheduler contention** (`pthread_cond_signal`) — per-record handoffs between workers and the serial reducer; the pipeline averages only ~1.2 cores despite being parallel.

## What this changes

1. **Your installed plugin is 2× stale.** Main is already 34s vs your 70s, at a third of the memory. Cheapest win available: upgrade.
2. **The biggest graph lever is the `full` profile's flow analysis, and Brain hardcodes `full`** (`semantic_stream.go:407` passes no `--profile`). `fast` is 10s and drops exactly the regex-heavy families (DATA_FLOWS, broad call fanout, evidence). Before switching Brain to `fast`, we need to check whether anything Brain serves (impact analysis in MCP, brief likely-files) actually consumes DATA_FLOWS — that's a one-grep question.
3. **Warm-path is already solved** — 1s, byte-identical, and Brain's invocation hits it. The cold-parse pain is per-commit-change only.
4. **With graph warm, Brain's own ingest (36s) is now the dominant pipeline cost** — 22s sqlite build plus re-serializing a 125MB stream into a 158MB file it keeps forever. That's the "second cache" question we queued next, and the numbers now frame it sharply: Brain spends 36s + 360MB + 1.8s/brief maintaining a copy of something graph serves in 1s.

Graph-side fix candidates, if you want them ranked: gate or optimize the flow-analysis regexes (single-pass scanner or tree-sitter queries instead of 600+ regex families), batch the reducer handoffs to kill the 28% scheduler tax, and parallelize Phase 2 harder. But honestly, point 4 is where the evidence points: the next conversation is the second cache, and these numbers mostly argue for Brain getting out of the snapshot-storage business.

content.text:
Full matrix against main is done — and it surfaced a second real bug.

## Baseline, everything on main (brain@main `eb-main` + graph@d35078de)

| Step | v0.4.0 (released) | main |
|---|---|---|
| graph parse full, cold | 70.7s / 1.53GB | **34.3s / 0.58GB** |
| graph parse fast / syntax-only, cold | 15.2s / 2.7s | 10.3s / 2.8s |
| graph parse, repeat run (cache) | **1.0s** | **34.4s — cache broken** |
| Brain `refresh index` end-to-end | ~36s (warm graph) | 69.5s (34s parse + 35s ingest, every time) |
| Brief, steady state | 4.0s | 4.2s (same shape: status 2.3s, semantic read 1.4s) |

## The new finding: main never caches large snapshots

Main replaced v0.4.0's unbounded cache tee with an in-memory buffer capped at **64MB** (`providerRecordsCacheMaxBytes`, `internal/cli/root.go:561`). Past the cap, the entry is **silently not stored**. This repo's full snapshot is 130MB — so on main, every snapshot re-parses from scratch; the 1.0s warm path you'd ship to users only exists below 64MB. Verified both directions: syntax-only (55MB) caches on main (3.6s → 0.48s), full (130MB) never does. The `fast` profile output (83MB) is *also* over the cap. The cap was a legitimate memory fix — v0.4.0 held the whole stream in RAM, part of its 1.53GB RSS — but the fix traded "caching works" for "memory bounded" when a disk-spooled gzip tee (entries are ~10MB gz on disk anyway) would give both.

So the net story for main today: parse is 2× faster and 2.6× leaner, **but** on any real repo you pay all 34s on every re-index, which makes Brain's end-to-end re-index ~70s per commit-change instead of ~36s.

## Unchanged from the earlier profile

CPU is 42% regex relation extraction (DATA_FLOWS flow analysis 17%, deep call resolution 10%), tree-sitter only 5.6%, 28% scheduler contention. Brain still hardcodes `--profile full` and its own ingest (35s: 23s sqlite build + 158MB re-serialization) is the other half of the pipeline. Also reconfirmed: the first brief after any refresh pays a one-time ~7.4s history-FTS rebuild.

Recommended fix order on the graph side: **(1)** the cache regression — disk-spooled gzip tee, no cap needed (restores the 1s warm path at bounded memory; biggest single lever and a straight bug); **(2)** gate or optimize the flow-analysis regexes (`fast` is already 3.3× cheaper if Brain doesn't need DATA_FLOWS — one grep to verify); **(3)** the reducer handoff contention. All three recorded in Brain. Want tickets for the cache regression (entire-graph repo) and the first-brief FTS cost (entire-brain)?

content.thinking:
Brain only uses DATA_FLOWS as a ranking boost, so it degrades gracefully if absent, falling back to CALLS/type edges, and the fast profile already relies on CALLS, types, and routes. I'm now checking whether the MCP impact_analysis path also depends on DATA_FLOWS.

Switching Brain to the fast profile looks viable, though the shallow call resolution could shrink impact analysis blast radius from dropped name-only fanout, so it's worth flagging in the ticket and deciding with an eval rather than assuming.

I'm drafting four graph/brain tickets: T1 for the cache regression needing disk-spooled gzip tee, T2 for gating or optimizing the costly flow-analysis regex (noting Brain's DATA_FLOWS usage is just a rank preference), T3 for reducer/scheduler contention from per-record handoffs that should batch between workers, and T4 for eagerly rebuilding the 7.4s history FTS index during refresh instead of on first brief. I'm figuring out these graph tickets belong in the Core team's Linear workspace.

Now for the "why is parsing slow" explanation: actual tree-sitter parsing is only ~5.6% (2s), confirmed by the syntax-only run finishing in 2.8s across all files. The real cost is the semantic enrichment phase, which re-reads every function body and fires hundreds of regex pattern matchers (614 compile sites) for flow analysis, call resolution, string constants, and routes — many hitting Go's regexp backtracking paths across ~52k symbol bodies — plus another 28% lost to scheduler overhead from per-record channel handoffs. So the intuition that this "should be faster" holds up: the real ceiling is the syntax-only time, and everything beyond that is avoidable regex and scheduling overhead.
Confirmed that Brain only uses DATA_FLOWS as an optional ranking preference, not a requirement, so `fast` works for Brain's ingest. Now creating the four tickets.

input.title: Graph: provider records cache silently never stores snapshots over 64MB — restore large-repo caching with a disk-spooled gzip tee
input.description:
## Problem

main's provider-records cache tee buffers the record stream uncompressed in memory, capped at `providerRecordsCacheMaxBytes = 64MB` (`internal/cli/root.go` ~561). Past the cap the buffer is released and the cache entry is silently not stored. Any repo whose snapshot stream exceeds 64MB therefore re-parses on every run.

Measured on entire-brain (1,817 files, snapshot 130MB), 2026-10-20:
- v0.4.0 (unbounded tee, always stored): repeat snapshot in **1.0s**, byte-identical, ~10MB gz entry.
- main (d35078de): repeat snapshot **34.4s** — no cache entry written, no warning.
- Control: `--profile syntax-only` (55MB, under the cap) caches fine on main (3.6s cold / 0.48s warm).

The `fast` profile output (83MB) is also over the cap. On large repos this is the 900s-timeout class: every Brain re-index pays a full re-parse.

The cap itself was a legitimate fix — v0.4.0 held the entire stream in RAM (part of its 1.53GB peak RSS vs main's 0.58GB). But it traded "caching works" for "memory bounded".

## Fix

Stream the tee through gzip into a temp file inside the cache directory and rename into place on success (the stored entries are ~10MB gz on disk already). Disk-backed spooling gives bounded memory with no size cap. Failure to spool stays best-effort, as today.

Also emit a one-line stderr notice when an entry is skipped or fails to store, so this class of regression is observable.

## Validation

- Repeat `snapshot --format ndjson` on a repo with a >64MB stream: second run must be ~1s and byte-identical.
- Peak RSS during the cold run must not grow with stream size.
- Regression test with a shrunken cap proving over-cap streams still get cached via the spool.

input.title: Graph: full-profile snapshot spends 42% of CPU in regex flow analysis — gate or optimize
input.description:
## Problem

CPU profile of a cold `snapshot --profile full` on entire-brain (main d35078de, 34.3s wall, pprof 40.4s samples):

- **42% in `forEachRelation` regex relation extraction**: `returnFlowCalls`/DATA_FLOWS 17%, `receiverCallRelations` 10%, `staticStringConstants` 5%, `expressionAssignedReturnFlows` 5%. Dominated by `regexp.tryBacktrack` and the regexp machine (the sem package has 614 regex compile sites; Phase 2 re-reads every function body and runs regex families over it).
- Tree-sitter parsing is only **5.6%** — the parser is not the cost; `--profile syntax-only` indexes the whole repo in 2.8s.
- Measured depth lever: full 34.3s, fast 10.3s, syntax-only 2.8s.

## Direction (either or both)

1. **Gate**: Brain hardcodes the default `full` profile (`entire-brain internal/cli/semantic_stream.go:407` passes no `--profile`). Verified: Brain's only DATA_FLOWS consumer is a rank *preference* (`agent_surface.go` `brainBriefRelationPriority`), nothing requires the edge; `fast` keeps high-precision CALLS, types, routes. Switching Brain's ingest to `fast` is a one-line change on the Brain side — caveat to check: `fast`'s shallow call resolution drops broad name-only call fanout, which may shrink impact-analysis blast radius.
2. **Optimize**: replace the per-family regex passes with a single-pass scanner or tree-sitter queries over the already-parsed tree. The bodies are already parsed once in Phase 1; re-scanning them with backtracking regexes in Phase 2 is the measured hotspot.

## Validation

- pprof before/after on the same repo; target full-profile cold under ~15s with unchanged relation output (or a documented, deliberate reduction).
- Relation count diff between old/new on a fixture repo.

input.title: Graph: snapshot pipeline loses ~28% of CPU to scheduler contention — batch worker/reducer handoffs
input.description:
## Problem

In the same cold-snapshot CPU profile (entire-brain repo, main d35078de), 28% of samples are scheduler overhead — `runtime.pthread_cond_signal` 27.7% flat plus `pthread_cond_wait`/`usleep` — from fine-grained handoffs between the parallel file workers, the ordered reducer, and per-record emission (`runIndexedStreamingPipeline`). The pipeline averages only ~1.2 cores on an 8+-core machine despite ≤8 workers (`boundedProviderWorkerCount`).

Wall-clock effect: 34.3s cold with 43s user — most cores idle most of the time.

## Direction

- Batch the worker→reducer channel to hand off chunks of records instead of one `providerFileResult`/record per signal.
- Consider buffering emission (the NDJSON encoder writes record-at-a-time through a mutexed writer).
- Re-check the worker cap: with contention fixed, >8 workers may pay off on large repos.

## Validation

pprof before/after: `pthread_cond_signal` flat share should drop to low single digits; cold wall time on entire-brain should approach CPU-time / cores. No output byte changes (the reducer's deterministic ordering contract must hold — snapshots are cache-keyed on byte identity).

input.title: Brain: first brief after any refresh pays ~7.4s degraded history ranking — rebuild the history FTS eagerly in refresh
input.description:
## Problem

After any `refresh`, the history BM25/FTS derivation is stale, and the next read query rebuilds it lazily. The first `brief` therefore ranks 183k history records on the degraded raw-scan path: measured `history.indexed_rank` = 7.4–7.9s on that first brief, vs ~145ms on every subsequent one (brief `--profile-json`, entire-brain repo, reproduced 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20).

Since refresh runs in the background (watch daemon) and brief is the agent-facing entry point, the cost lands on exactly the latency-sensitive call.

## Fix

Rebuild (or incrementally update) the history FTS derivation at the end of refresh, where the latency is invisible, instead of handing it to the next reader. Same policy as the other derived projections refresh already rebuilds.

## Validation

`refresh && brief --profile-json`: first brief's `history.indexed_rank` should be ~150ms, not seconds. One regression test asserting the FTS derivation is current immediately after refresh.

content.text:
Four tickets filed, in your order:

- [COR-2196](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2196) — cache regression: bring caching back as a disk-spooled gzip tee (yes, exactly "back in a better form": v0.4.0's behavior, without its unbounded memory)
- [COR-2197](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2197) — gate/optimize the regex flow analysis (includes the verified fact: Brain only uses DATA_FLOWS as a rank preference, so `fast` is safe for Brain's ingest, with one caveat on impact blast-radius to check)
- [COR-2198](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2198) — batch the worker/reducer handoffs (28% scheduler tax)
- [COR-2199](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2199) — Brain: rebuild history FTS eagerly in refresh so the first brief stops paying 7.4s

**Why the parse is slow:** your instinct is right — the *parsing* is fast. `syntax-only` processes all 1,817 files in 2.8s, and in the CPU profile tree-sitter is 5.6% of the work. The other ~90% is what happens after parsing: the pipeline re-reads every function body in Phase 2 and runs families of Go regexes over it to *infer* semantic edges — "does this callee's return value flow into the caller's return" (DATA_FLOWS), receiver-based call resolution, string constants, route literals. The sem package has 614 compiled regexes, many hitting Go's backtracking path (`tryBacktrack` alone is 27% cumulative), applied per-function across 52k symbols. It's hundreds of small pattern matchers × tens of thousands of bodies. On top of that, the pipeline only achieves ~1.2 cores because workers and the ordered reducer signal each other per record.

So the honest decomposition of 34s: ~2s parsing, ~14s regex flow/call inference, ~10s lost to contention, the rest in emission/GC. That's why the fix order is what it is: 2196 makes repeat cost 1s again (the number users actually feel), 2197 attacks the inference cost itself, 2198 recovers the idle cores.

content.content:
# AGENTS.md — operating guide for coding agents

Hand this to any coding agent working in a repo where the `entire graph` plugin
is installed. It moves initial code-location work from broad grep/read
exploration to targeted graph queries. Token impact depends on the task and the
model, so treat any single figure as scenario-dependent; the measured range and
the conditions behind it are in the [README](README.md).

Two guidance surfaces coexist here on purpose. `.entire/agent-guide.md` is the
generated activation artifact — regenerated in full by `init-agents`, so never
edit it by hand — and is what agents load through the managed block at the end
of this file. This document is the maintained long-form reference; its examples
pass flags explicitly (such as `--format text`) for readability rather than
relying on command defaults.

## What this gives you

A precomputed code graph is available through the `entire graph` command — functions, classes, methods, types, routes, and the calls/inheritance/field/service relations between them, parsed with tree-sitter. Built-in analysis is local and no-egress (no network, no model, no keys). Use it to **LOCATE** and **UNDERSTAND** code when additional discovery is needed. The same repository view and options yield the same graph, but static relations can be heuristic or incomplete; inspect focused source and verify the resulting change. Some commands write derivative caches or explicitly requested setup/report files; inspect command help when filesystem writes matter.

Default flags to remember: pass `--repo .` when you're not inside an Entire session. The interactive query family (`query`, `def`, `explain`, `neighbors`, and `impact`) reads your **working tree by default** so uncommitted edits are visible; `--head` switches those commands to committed-tree semantics. Other command families have different defaults.

---

## The parts of the graph

Reach for the smallest tool that answers your question.

### 🔍 query — *find the code for a task* (when discovery is needed)
Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with the source and `file:line` inline. Hybrid ranking over bodies, identifiers (camelCase/snake_case aware), signatures, paths, and graph neighbors. Output is byte-budgeted to drop straight into context.

```sh
entire graph query --repo . --query "<the task or bug in one plain sentence>" --format text --top-k 8
```

- `--format agent` for compact ranked output with latency telemetry; `json`/`ndjson` for the full schema (completeness, partial failures, diagnostics).
- `--top-k N` result count; `--max-context-bytes N` byte budget (`0` = unbounded).
- Working tree by default (always rebuilt and never cached); add `--head` for cached committed-tree semantics.
- `--profile syntax-only|fast|full` (default `fast`); `--index-all-files` or `--max-indexed-files N` to widen/bound cold-search parsing.

**When:** additional code discovery is needed; reuse locations already supplied by the task or Brain brief.

### 🕸️ neighbors — *who calls this / what does it call* (targeted relations)
Direct incoming/outgoing relations for **one** symbol, with definition locations, plus bounded two-hop paths at `--depth 2`. For the full blast radius of a change, prefer `impact`; use `neighbors` when you want one specific relation/direction. Never `edges` for this (full stream).

```sh
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol NAME --relation CALLS --direction in   # who calls NAME
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol NAME --relation CALLS --direction out  # what NAME calls
```

- `--file path` — **required** when the symbol name is ambiguous (multiple defs); the graph returns definitions only until you disambiguate.
- `--relation CALLS` (default is the call family) — pick another relation to follow it instead.
- `--direction both|in|out`, `--depth 1|2`, `--limit N`.
- `--internal-only` drops unresolved external endpoints; `--exclude-tests` drops test-only neighbors.
- `--format agent|text|json`; `--head` for cached committed-tree; `--profile fast` for shallow call resolution (default `full` favors correctness).

**When:** "what breaks if I change X", "who uses this", tracing a call chain — after query has given you a concrete symbol name.

### 💥 impact — *one-shot blast radius for a change*
Everything the graph knows about changing **one** symbol, in a single bounded explanation: direct + transitive callers (depth ≤ 2), callees, type consumers (`USES_TYPE`/`PARAM_TYPE`/`RETURNS_TYPE`), data flows, files that historically change together with the symbol's file, and same-container siblings. Text output is sectioned, `file:line` per entry, capped per section and ~4 KB total.

---CLAUDE---
@AGENTS.md

<!-- entire-agent:begin -->
<!-- Entire agent instructions are inherited through AGENTS.md. -->
<!-- entire-agent:end -->

## What this gives you

A precomputed code graph is available through the `entire graph` command — functions, classes, methods, types, routes, and the calls/inheritance/field/service relations between them, parsed with tree-sitter. Built-in analysis is local and no-egress (no network, no model, no keys). Use it to **LOCATE** and **UNDERSTAND** code when additional discovery is needed. The same repository view and options yield the same graph, but static relations can be heuristic or incomplete; inspect focused source and verify the resulting change. Some commands write derivative caches or explicitly requested setup/report files; inspect command help when filesystem writes matter.

Default flags to remember: pass `--repo .` when you're not inside an Entire session. The interactive query family (`query`, `def`, `explain`, `neighbors`, and `impact`) reads your **working tree by default** so uncommitted edits are visible; `--head` switches those commands to committed-tree semantics. Other command families have different defaults.

---

## The parts of the graph

Reach for the smallest tool that answers your question.

### 🔍 query — *find the code for a task* (when discovery is needed)
Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with the source and `file:line` inline. Hybrid ranking over bodies, identifiers (camelCase/snake_case aware), signatures, paths, and graph neighbors. Output is byte-budgeted to drop straight into context.

```sh
entire graph query --repo . --query "<the task or bug in one plain sentence>" --format text --top-k 8
```

- `--format agent` for compact ranked output with latency telemetry; `json`/`ndjson` for the full schema (completeness, partial failures, diagnostics).
- `--top-k N` result count; `--max-context-bytes N` byte budget (`0` = unbounded).
- Working tree by default (always rebuilt and never cached); add `--head` for cached committed-tree semantics.
- `--profile syntax-only|fast|full` (default `fast`); `--index-all-files` or `--max-indexed-files N` to widen/bound cold-search parsing.

**When:** additional code discovery is needed; reuse locations already supplied by the task or Brain brief.

### 🕸️ neighbors — *who calls this / what does it call* (targeted relations)
Direct incoming/outgoing relations for **one** symbol, with definition locations, plus bounded two-hop paths at `--depth 2`. For the full blast radius of a change, prefer `impact`; use `neighbors` when you want one specific relation/direction. Never `edges` for this (full stream).

```sh
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol NAME --relation CALLS --direction in   # who calls NAME
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol NAME --relation CALLS --direction out  # what NAME calls
```

- `--file path` — **required** when the symbol name is ambiguous (multiple defs); the graph returns definitions only until you disambiguate.
- `--relation CALLS` (default is the call family) — pick another relation to follow it instead.
- `--direction both|in|out`, `--depth 1|2`, `--limit N`.
- `--internal-only` drops unresolved external endpoints; `--exclude-tests` drops test-only neighbors.
- `--format agent|text|json`; `--head` for cached committed-tree; `--profile fast` for shallow call resolution (default `full` favors correctness).

**When:** "what breaks if I change X", "who uses this", tracing a call chain — after query has given you a concrete symbol name.

### 💥 impact — *one-shot blast radius for a change*
Everything the graph knows about changing **one** symbol, in a single bounded explanation: direct + transitive callers (depth ≤ 2), callees, type consumers (`USES_TYPE`/`PARAM_TYPE`/`RETURNS_TYPE`), data flows, files that historically change together with the symbol's file, and same-container siblings. Text output is sectioned, `file:line` per entry, capped per section and ~4 KB total.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.
